name: Life Sciences
blurb: How pharma, biotech and medtech use AI, from discovery and trials to regulation, manufacturing and safety.
title: Life Sciences
answer: Life sciences companies now use AI at every stage of a medicine's life: to find targets and design molecules, to run and analyse trials, to write regulatory documents, to control manufacturing and to watch for safety signals. Regulators have moved from discussion papers to concrete rules, and the first AI designed drugs are reaching late stage trials.

sections.body: AI is no longer a side project in this industry. The regulators now expect a documented case for every model that touches a submission, a batch record or a safety decision, so the work that matters most is governance: knowing which models are in use, what each is trusted to do, and how that trust was established.
sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences team

developments.text: The FDA and the European Medicines Agency issued ten shared guiding principles for good AI practice across drug development, manufacturing and pharmacovigilance, the first joint statement of its kind.

sources.title: FDA, Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice in Drug Development
EMA, EMA and FDA set common principles for AI in medicine development

developments.text: Eli Lilly and NVIDIA announced a joint AI co-innovation lab for drug discovery, built on NVIDIA's BioNeMo framework and its Vera Rubin hardware.

sources.title: Lilly, NVIDIA and Lilly announce co-innovation AI lab

developments.text: Insilico Medicine published phase 2a results in Nature Medicine for rentosertib, a drug whose target and molecule were both found with AI, showing improved lung function in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis over 12 weeks.
The FDA published its first draft guidance on using AI to support regulatory decisions for drugs and biologics, built on a seven step, risk based credibility framework.

sources.title: FDA, Considerations for the Use of AI to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products
